title: Training randomness may not vary with the run seed (trainer seed fixed at 42)
quote: 0, weight decay 0, gradient clipping 1.0 and trainer seed 42, all library defaults
explanation: Section 3.3 defines a seed as setting the exam partition, selection set and training randomness at once, and Section 3.4 says Python/torch seeds are set from the run seed. But the trainer seed is stated as fixed at 42 (a library default). In HF/TRL the Trainer re-seeds at construction, which typically overrides earlier global seeding, so LoRA initialisation and data order may be identical across all runs. If so, 'seeds' vary only the partition and sampling, and the claims about training-seed variance (the replicate pair, the 3-seed final round, the B-A sign flip attributed to 'trajectory noise') are not measuring what they say. The paper never says which seed governs adapter init and shuffling, so the reader cannot tell what the 'seed-to-seed' spread includes.

title: The 'replicate pair' conflates exam-partition change with training noise
explanation: Section 3.3 says repeating A and B at a second seed 'draws a different 150-problem exam set' (the quoted sentence is 'since the seed also sets the train/exam partition, the repetition draws a different 150-problem exam set'). Section 3.4 then calls the A (or B) seed-0/seed-1 pair 'the one same-configuration replicate pair' whose sample accuracy ends 3.2 points apart, and uses 3.2 as the measure of training-seed variance (also in the detectable-effect paragraph, and 'closer to two replicates' for same-seed A/B in 4.4). A pair that differs in exam set, selection set and (possibly) training randomness is not a replicate of training noise: the 3.2 mixes partition sampling (including the 11-18 unparseable golds per partition) with training variance. It is also a single pair, so it cannot support a variance estimate or the statement that intervals omit seed variance by a known amount. The paper should say which pair is meant and what varies.

title: Detectable-effect rule is applied loosely and its conclusion is stated in the wrong direction
quote: these are lower bounds: a null here means no
explanation: The rule 'exceeded about 2.8 h/1.96' is the standard (z_{0.975}+z_{0.8})*SE with SE=h/1.96, assuming a normal approximation and that the paired-bootstrap h of an observed change represents the sampling SD of the test. That is acceptable as a rough guide, but (i) h is estimated from the very runs being judged (post hoc power), and pass@1 rests on one draw per problem with 150 problems, where a percentile bootstrap half-width is crude; (ii) h comes from Table 2 (Design I at 1e-5, k=8) yet the same figures are then used for the k=4 high-rate runs and the pass@k column, whose h differ; (iii) the text says the numbers are lower bounds on the detectable effect and then concludes 'a null here means no gain of at least that size, probably larger'. If the true minimum detectable effect is larger than stated, a null excludes only gains larger than that larger value, so 'no gain of at least that size' is not supported; it is the opposite of what a lower bound on detectability implies. A null result also never excludes an effect at 80% power in the sense used. Finally, the observed declines of 1.2-3.2 points in sample accuracy are below the stated 3.5-5.5 detectable range yet are called excluding zero, which is consistent only if the rule is a power statement and not a significance rule; the paper should state this.

title: Bootstrap and interval procedures are inconsistently or incompletely specified
quote: 95% interval from a paired problem-level bootstrap (10,000 resamples of the
explanation: Section 3.4 describes a bootstrap over 'the 150 exam problems', but Table 5 resamples all 500 problems (2,000 resamples), the final round uses a 500-problem exam, and Section 4.6 reports t-intervals over three loop seeds; none of these latter procedures (t-interval with 2 degrees of freedom, resampling unit across seeds, what is paired) is defined in the setup. Bootstrapping conditional on one fixed exam partition does not cover partition (problem-draw) variation across seeds although the paper uses different partitions per seed; and 'respects the clustering of the k samples' holds for sample accuracy but pass@1 uses one sample per problem and so also contains within-problem sampling noise that is not separable. 'Matched' and 'audit' columns use 2,000 resamples with no reason for the change. A percentile interval from 150 problems with many all-fail problems (about half) is also not obviously well calibrated for pass@k near boundaries. These choices affect nearly every 'interval includes zero' claim, so they should be fully specified.

title: Unparseable golds: 'always unsolved' under V conflicts with the V' re-scoring and the 5.3 audit
quote: 500 stored MATH-500 golds (10.2%); these problems always count as unsolved,
explanation: Section 3.2 says the 51 unparseable golds can never be solved or enter the pool (under V) and that offsets are not cancelled across partitions. The V' paragraph then says 29-34 of the 54-62 problems where the storage defect fires 'have a gold the original verifier cannot parse at all, so no answer form avoids it there', and Section 5.3 repeats this. But V' by definition wraps the gold in \boxed{}, which then parses, so these problems are solvable under V'. Hence they are not a defect that 'no answer form' avoids; they are problems where V's bare gold parse fails and V' repairs it. This blurs two distinct defects (bare-gold parse failure vs. delimiter-dependent extraction) in the single '15.5-18.3% false reject' figure, and the headline 'lowers pass@1 by 4.7-8.0' mixes them. It also leaves unclear how 51 unparseable golds relate to the 29-34: the remaining 17-22 unparseable golds never fire (V' also fails? model never boxes?), which is not stated, and the remaining 'parseable' 24-28 problems in 5.3 are the only ones where avoidance is possible, which is a far smaller basis than the 15.5-18.3% suggests for adaptation. The statement that offsets cancel 'only if those problems would not otherwise change' is also untested and sits in tension with the paper's reliance on within-run differences.
source_section: 3.2 The Verifier and Its Directional Bias

title: Definition of V' and the 'five runs re-scored' statement are ambiguous and mixed across run types
quote: Re-scored, sample accuracy still falls in all
explanation: V' is defined conditionally on each prediction ('wraps the gold in \boxed{} when the prediction contains one'), so the gold differs per prediction and V' is not a fixed alternative verifier; how a prediction with \boxed in an intermediate step, multiple boxes, or \boxed absent but $...$ present is handled is not specified. The sentence 'sample accuracy still falls in all five runs we re-scored' is then used with a 0.73-0.85 original-to-rescored ratio; Table 5 shows the five re-scored runs are three self-training runs and two train-on-gold runs (whose accuracy collapse is the failed gate), while Section 5.3 speaks of 'all three self-training runs'. The reader cannot tell whether the ratio and the 'still falls' claim cover gold runs and runs at different k and rate (1e-5 k=8 vs 5e-4 k=4), nor which seed/partition each belongs to; the range 15.5-18.3% mixes round-0 and last-round values (Table 5 round 0 is 18.0-18.3). 'Rejects 15.5-18.3% of the generations V' accepts' is therefore not a single well-defined quantity. Also, the 7.8% false-negative rate (Qwen2.5-7B, 128 problems) and this 15-18% rate are different measurements that the text equates only through 'probably'.

title: Primary-metric choice and pass@1 definition create post hoc exposure and cross-section inconsistency
quote: set measures, but it estimates the same quantity from all k samples with less
explanation: Section 3.4 states that pass@1 (first of k samples) was preregistered, sample accuracy was chosen as primary after seeing runs, and the 2.2-point bound rests on it. Meanwhile the detectability claims, the 'about 10 points' power statement, and Table 1/2 headline comparisons mix pass@1 (noisy, one draw), pass@k (any-of-k, which differs between k=8 and k=4 runs and so is not comparable across Design I and the higher-rate runs) and sample accuracy. Choosing the metric after observing that it gave tighter intervals (and, in the 4.4 runs, intervals excluding zero) is exactly the multiplicity/forking-paths issue the paper says it does not correct for, yet declines are read with sample-accuracy intervals as 'excluding zero'. Also 'pass@k' is the plug-in any-of-k rate, not the unbiased estimator, so changing k changes the estimand across rows. The paper should apply to itself the same standard (preregistered metric, multiplicity) it uses to discount gains.

title: Training loss on the prompt and truncation to 512 tokens confound the loop and the 'null' interpretation
quote: from the run seed; loss over the whole chat sequence, prompt included; fp16 on
explanation: The setup trains with loss over the prompt as well, a 512-token limit that includes the prompt, and 24-26% of the round-0 pool cut so that the final answer and EOS are removed. These are not minor settings: with a quarter of the training targets lacking the answer and termination, the loop teaches truncated outputs, and prompt-token loss dilutes the signal. The paper acknowledges this later (and the final round changes it), but Section 3 presents the recipe as 'the' GVT loop and the title/claims describe a null for 'one recipe' while Sections 3.1-3.4 never state why these defaults are a fair test; the 'not tuned, default of our code' rationale for the learning rate is given, but none for loss masking, rank, target modules, or the 512 cap. This affects what a null can mean and is the main reason the gate fails, so the setup should flag it as a recipe defect rather than leave it to Section 4.5.
